blocks.text: **The problem.** A tree with `n` vertices, labelled `1` to `n`, had **one extra edge** added, so now there are `n` edges and exactly one cycle. Given the `edges` in order, return an edge you can remove to get a tree back. If several would work, return the one that appears **last** in the input.

blocks.alt: Five vertices. Edges 1-2, 2-3, 3-4 and 1-5 form a tree; the edge 1-4, in red, closes the loop 1, 2, 3, 4. Removing it leaves a tree again.

blocks.text: Some questions are about **groups that merge**: which vertices are connected so far, are these two in the same group, join these two groups. A **Union-Find** (also called a *disjoint set union*) answers them almost instantly, even while edges keep arriving — no search needed.
Each group is stored as a little tree in one array, `parent`. Every vertex points at its parent, and the **root** — the vertex that points at itself — names the group. Two operations:

items: **find(x)** — climb parent pointers from `x` to the root. Two vertices are in the same group exactly when they have the same root.
**union(x, y)** — find both roots; if they differ, point one root at the other. The two trees, and so the two groups, become one.

blocks.alt: Two groups stored as trees: 2 and 3 point at root 1; 5 points at root 4. union(3, 5) finds roots 1 and 4 and points 4 at 1, so all five vertices are now one group with root 1.

blocks.text: Two small tricks keep the trees flat. **Union by size**: hang the smaller tree under the bigger one, so trees grow wide, not tall. **Path halving**: while `find` climbs, point each vertex at its grandparent, so the next climb is shorter. With both, each operation takes O(α(n)) — α is the inverse Ackermann function, which is below 5 for any input that fits in a computer. In practice: constant time.
Here, the question is exactly *were these two already connected?* Add the edges in order; the first edge whose two ends already share a root closes the cycle.
1. Brute force: search before every edge
Before adding edge `u - v`, run a DFS to see whether `u` can already reach `v`. If it can, this edge makes a second route between them: it's the redundant one.
**Time O(n²), space O(n).** Each of the n edges may search the whole graph built so far. The same question — *already connected?* — is answered from scratch every time.
Start with every vertex in its own group. For each edge, find the roots of both ends. Different roots: union the groups. The same root: the ends were already connected, so return this edge.

blocks.caption: Groups merge as edges arrive; watch the parent pointers form trees. The edge whose ends share a root is the answer.

blocks.text: **Time O(n · α(n)), space O(n).** Each edge does two `find`s and at most one union, each practically constant. Why is the first edge that closes a cycle also the *last* one on it in the input? Every other edge of the cycle was added before it without closing anything.

blocks.alt: Search per edge: O(n²) time, O(n) space. Union-Find: O(n·α(n)) time, O(n) space.

blocks.text: Union-Find wins whenever edges arrive one at a time and the question is *connected yet?* A DFS has to search again after every edge; Union-Find just remembers the groups.

items: **The smallest cycle** — `[[1,2],[1,3],[2,3]]` returns `[2,3]`, the last edge of the triangle.
**Order matters** — the answer is the cycle edge that comes last in the input, whatever the vertex numbers are.
**Long chains** — without union by size or path halving, `find` can walk a chain of n vertices every time and the whole thing becomes O(n²).
**Vertices numbered from 1** — size the arrays `n + 1` and ignore index 0.
**Number of Provinces** — union every pair of connected cities and count the roots. (Pattern 1 did it with DFS.)
**Graph Valid Tree** — exactly n - 1 edges, and no edge ever finds both ends already joined.
**Redundant Connection II** — the directed version: a vertex may end up with two parents, which needs extra case analysis on top of Union-Find.
